title.narrative: Soil Values

description.narrative: Soil Values aims to enable small-scale food producers in the Sahel (women, men, and youth) to sustainably manage soil fertility to improve ecologically sustainable food production and increase resilience to climate change and shocks. More concretely, in terms of impact, after 10 years of implementation, Soil Values will ensure that sustainable soil fertility management is a mainstay of farming systems in the Sahel, improving the soil fertility and production capacity of 2 million hectares of farmland in the Sahel, as well as the resilience and well-being of 1.5 million small-scale food producers, particularly women, in Burkina Faso, Mali, Niger and northern Nigeria

Soil Values is a 10-tear program that will work through three pathways to change, each representing a different area of action (1) the agroecological pathway, (2) the inclusive market development pathway (markets and finance), and (3) the enabling environment pathway (institutions and policies). The agroecological pathway targets small-scale food producers and farming systems, as well as the landscapes and watersheds that surround them. The inclusive market development path focuses on the private sector (markets, investments, business models) to overcome market barriers and strengthen relevant markets, and on financing institutions to invest in soil fertility. Finally, the enabling environment pathway focuses on the ability of public sector institutions, policies, and governance structures to support soil health in the long term.
Soil Values targets small-scale food producers, particularly women and youth, in Burkina Faso, Mali, Niger and Nigeria (northern)

Soil Values will work through the following five areas of intervention:1-Bundling: grouping of technical and socio-economic interventions into combined packages to address soil fertility management at farm level in the broadest possible sense. 2-Integrate our interventions at landscape and watershed level to optimize water management and nutrient use efficiency, introduce nature-based solutions for landscape greening, and create participatory, co-designed plans at community level for sustainable natural resource management. 3-Brokering for long-term investment in soil fertility management, and identifying payment mechanisms for small-scale food producers, including livestock farmers and breeders. 4-Convening to stimulate a favorable policy environment at regional, national, and sub-national levels. 5-Scoping and learning to integrate lessons learned from the program and other initiatives, and build capacity of key stakeholders.

Impact: Small-scale food producers in the Sahel (women, men, and youth) sustainably manage soil fertility to improve ecologically sustainable food production and increase resilience to climate change and shocks.
B.1.3. Number of female small scale food producers who become progressively empowered

description.narrative: Empowerment – as an outcome – can be understood as ‘the degree of freedom people have to control and have positive impacts on their lives and futures’ (Elias et al., 2021*). As a process, empowerment refers to changes in institutions and (resource) access that contribute to such freedom. We thus take this indicator to refer to the number of female SSFPs (as participants in NL-funded activities) who experience increased freedom to make life choices and access resources, in particular those related to agricultural production and to nutrition

title.narrative: D.1. Number of small-scale food producers applying new technologies/practices that aim to transform food systems towards desirable outcomes

description.narrative: Application of new technologies/practices refers to putting into use knowledge, inputs (seeds, fertilizer), machinery, cropping schemes and cultivation methods that are new to the SSFP concerned. The reference to desirable outcomes is added in order to filter for adoption of technologies/practices that are potentially beneficial.

title.narrative: B.1.4. Number of small scale food producers whose livelihood became more resilient to shocks

description.narrative: Resilience of food producers’ (farmers’) livelihoods to stresses and shocks refers to their capacity to resist, recover from, and/or adjust to disruptions and stresses that (may) adversely affect their livelihoods (e.g. climate/environmental, economic and social shocks). Livelihoods refers to farming-, income earning- and other activities that food producers and their households carry out to provide for their needs. Resilience can be addressed and targeted in many ways: Income diversification; crop diversification; early (hazard) warning systems; storage facilities; structural safety nets or insurance (e.g. savings groups). This indicator thus refers to the number of SSFPs with an increased capacity to maintain, recover or adjust their livelihood base – with a view to maintaining their engagement in food production – when faced with shocks or stresses.

title.narrative: Outcome 3: Soil fertility policies, strategies and capacities are strengthened at national, regional and civil society organization levels.
D.2. Number of FNS-relevant knowledge and extension institutions reached with interventions that aim to strengthen their capacity

description.narrative: Knowledge and extension institutes include universities, research institutes, TVET, extension services with at least national coverage. Interventions to strengthen their capacity can be advice, training, providing equipment or any other form of support to their institutional/organizational development.

title.narrative: E.1. Number of reforms/improvements in major (inter)national FNS policies/laws/regulations

description.narrative: Reforms or improvements can be any change in policies/laws/regulations, on condition that it can be made plausible that at least tens of thousands of undernourished people and/or small scale food producers potentially benefit from this change.

title.narrative: Outcome 1 : Small-scale food producers, in particular women, sustainably decrease the yield gap.
B.2.1. Number of SSFPs directly reached with activities aimed at structural/systemic improvement of their agricultural performance

description.narrative: Number of SSFPs directly reached with activities aimed at structural/systemic improvement of their agricultural performance Food producers reached in a targeted way (i.e. the people who are reached are – or can be – identified) with an intervention that structurally and/or systemically contributes to improving their agricultural performance (i.e. aimed at long-term outcome results, as formulated in the IGG-FNS framework). This can for instance be because the intervention covers multiple aspects of agricultural performance (inputs, farming techniques, market potential) and/or there is regular follow-up. Examples: integrated farmer support, e.g. combining training, inputs and access to markets.

title.narrative: B.1.1 Number of small scale food producers who progressively increase farming net income

description.narrative: This indicator refers to the number of SSFPs who raise their income towards a living income* for their household. The income increase should be at least 10% (see also under Methodology/Calculation). Farm income includes income from crop production, livestock production, fisheries and aquaculture production, and from forestry production. Here, (gross) income is given by the revenues from such production minus the operating costs of production.*A living income can be defined as the net annual income required for a household in a particular place to afford a decent standard of living for all members of that household. This mainly includes food, water, housing, education, clothing and costs for unforeseen events. Obviously, this means that what can be considered a ‘living income’ differs per (country) context.

title.narrative: B.1.2. Number of small scale food producers who progressively decrease the yield gap

description.narrative: This indicator refers to the number of SSFPs who structurally raise their average crop yield towards the potential yield, thus diminishing the yield gap*. The yield increase should be at least 20% (see also under Methodology/Calculation). Note that closing yield gaps completely is neither realistic nor desirable, as raising yields by means of more/improved inputs is generally no longer cost-effective and potentially not ecologically sustainable beyond a certain point.

title.narrative: Outcome 2: FARMLAND IS CONVERTED TO ECOLOGICALLY SUSTAINABLE USE
C.2.1. Number of hectares of farmland directly reached with activities aimed at structural/systemic improvement of agro-ecological sustainability

description.narrative: Number of hectares of farmland directly reached with activities aimed at structural/systemic improvement of agro-ecological sustainability Hectares of farmland reached in a targeted way (i.e. farmland area reached is – or can be – known) with an intervention that structurally and/or systemically contributes to improving ecologically sustainable land use (i.e. aimed at longterm outcome results, as formulated in the IGG-FNS framework). This can for instance be because the intervention covers multiple aspects of sustainable land use (soil fertility, biodiversity, crop rotation) and/or there is regular follow-up. Examples: targeted farmer training and inputs for climate-smart agriculture (CSA), integrated soil fertility management, crop rotation, erosion protection measures, (…)

title.narrative: C.1.1. Number of hectares of farmland under at least 2 conservation practices

description.narrative: Agricultural (and livestock/fish farming) conservation practices refer to farming methods and techniques that not only facilitate efficient food production, but also prevent losses of land and water, safeguard natural resources, and promote biodiversity. These include - but are not limited to - the main principles of ‘conservation agriculture’ (CA): • minimal soil disturbance (e.g. no-tillage) • permanent soil cover (e.g. crops supplemented with organic matter) • crop diversification (e.g. through rotation or intercropping). Reference for qualifying practices is the Global Database on Sustainable Land Management (WOCAT). Not all these conservation practices may be applicable or relevant everywhere, thus locally appropriate practices may be selected and supported. This indicator thus refers to the amount of farmland (in hectares)* that is structurally under at least 2 conservation practices – of which at least 1 is new (i.e. practices that were not or only minimally exercised before). Note: this concerns practices exercised in such a way that they target a measurable improvement of agro-ecological conditions (e.g. soil quality, water infiltration or regenerative capacity). *Including pastures and fishing grounds (e.g. rotational grazing can be a conservation practice for livestock farming)

title.narrative: C.1.2. Number of hectares of farmland that agro-ecologically became more resilient to shocks

description.narrative: Agro-ecological resilience refers to the capacity of farmland to recover from disturbances such as extreme weather events, diseases and pests, generally through the maintenance of a functional balance of natural elements in and around the farmed area. This can be regarded as a form of buffer capacity. Such capacity can be present to varying extents on areas of farmland, which can be assessed by means of more specific indicators (see below under methodology / calculation).
